thesis: The problem was never a shortage of ambition; it was that ambition was spent on the machine instead of through it. Measured in this worktree 2026-09-02: 172 session files and 1 that touches a venture; 858 commits; 45,430 lines of docs; and 30,446 lines of test code against 16,839 lines of producing script, a 1.8:1 ratio of verification to production. So the anti-roadmap's job is to make growth conditional on external output, and to notice that most of the ~420-item catalogue does not need refusing on judgement — the smallest honest version of this company simply does not have the problems those items solve. Four of the twelve never-named gaps DISSOLVE under refusals (transcripts-as-memory, what-to-do-next, worker trust, self-explanation), three are already half-built, and of the five that are real work two are deferrable — leaving exactly the three STARTUP-OS §8 already named: goals, the loop, hands. The smallest thing that deserves the name company holds one mission across sessions, dispatches one move with fresh context, produces with real hands, stops itself on budget or stall, records every row against a task id, has a done-test resolved by something that is not the producer, and asks the world whether it worked while reporting `unresolved` when it cannot check. That is six mechanisms out of ~420, or 1.4%. Think big is not refused, it is relocated: to the depth of the goal tree, to distance travelled per human touch, and to the fifteen hands already bought and currently broken. The mechanism list is the one thing that gets a ceiling.

positions.claim: The smallest system that deserves the name 'company' is five state files and six mechanisms, and its defining property is the list of things it deliberately cannot do: run two missions, judge quality, learn from its transcripts, hold a persistent worker, speak, spend money, or reach a stranger without a human clearing a `blocking-human` gate.
positions.reasoning: The framing's three properties map to three implementations and no more. Runs unattended = the loop plus budget-guard's rope and stall ceiling plus a kill-switch file. Produces something = one pack (tools grant + done + stop_after) with fresh context per move. Knows whether it worked = a done-test whose resolver is never the producer, plus `verified_by: world` fail-closed. State lives in MISSIONS.yml (one in_flight ever), BOARD.md, packs/*.yml, .out-of-scope/, and an event log where every row carries a task id from the first row. L1 is kept unchanged. The cannot-do list is the load-bearing half, because each line is a problem the system therefore does not need to solve — a WIP limit of one eliminates the priority-function problem outright rather than deferring it.

positions.claim: The demand trigger: nothing new merges unless the same diff contains a caller AND that caller resolves to a mission in MISSIONS.yml with state in_flight carrying a `blocked` row that names the missing capability, authored before the diff.
positions.reasoning: X1's birth certificate prevents built-and-never-wired. It does not prevent built-and-wired-to-nothing-anyone-needed, which is the failure mode of nine phases: six of ten things the founder asked for already existed and were connected to nothing, so the wire is necessary and not sufficient. The trigger converts 'think big' from a plan into a queue — the catalogue does not shrink, it waits. Honest weakness, stated rather than discovered: this is the most gameable proposal here, since anyone with repo-write can author a mission and a block. It is the same bounded guarantee qa-lead-pass.yml already documents about itself — hash-bound, not signed — and it stops drift, not a determined author. The forced five predate any mission, so the bootstrap exemption must be a ledger claim with a valid_until, expiring rather than drifting.

positions.claim: Take the five headline open-source projects as ideas and refuse all five as dependencies in year one: beads, Temporal, pyribs/ShinkaEvolve, inspect_ai, projectmem.
positions.reasoning: Each is better in isolation than what we would write, and each introduces a second source of truth for something this system already computes: beads duplicates MISSIONS.yml, Temporal duplicates the loop's own record, projectmem duplicates the ledger's shape, inspect_ai duplicates the panel, and pyribs searches an archive that does not yet exist. A5 names the failure — two implementations will disagree and you find out during the incident — and this repo has lived it once already when qa-lead-pass.yml computed a stricter second tier than the classifier. The sharper reason is psychological rather than architectural: an unwired dependency is worse than an unimplemented idea because it looks done, and a package.json entry manufactures the feeling of capability at zero capability. Built-and-never-wired is present in four of four studied systems; adding dependencies is the cheapest way to make more of it.

positions.claim: Refuse worker trust, apprenticeship, promotion, demotion and retirement. Adopt T6, the competing position: no trust at all, only reach. The grant is the entire trust model.
positions.reasoning: Three converging reasons and the third is decisive. First, open-source.md §16 records that nothing in the surveyed world implements it — a genuine build, not a buy — making it the highest-cost, lowest-precedent item in the catalogue. Second, trust is a statistical object needing a volume of outcomes year one will not produce. Third, the architecture removes the subject: fresh context per unit of work plus a pack that is a grant and a stop means there is no persistent worker for trust to accrue to. What varies between two dispatches is the grant, and the grant is already the security boundary — an agent cannot research its way into holding a tool it was not granted. This is what makes the refusal load-bearing rather than prudent: gap #10 is not deferred, it is answered.

positions.claim: Refuse phase numbers. Continuous landings, each useful alone — and this position is the argument for why the founder's cadence decision is load-bearing rather than stylistic.
positions.reasoning: Omnigent shipped fifteen releases in ten weeks with no vendor harness ever dropped, and the phrase 'Phase N' appears nowhere in its changelog. This repo organises around phases and rewrites and has nine phases and one venture task. A phase number is a promise that a set of work ships together, which makes the last item hostage to the first, and makes a phase that turns out to be wrong expensive to abandon because abandoning it means admitting the number was wrong. Continuous landings carry no such hostage. Mechanism: WISH. There is no check for a phase number in a plan document and inventing a prose-vocabulary lint would be theatre. What makes it real is P3's demand trigger — work that must justify itself against a live mission cannot be batched into a phase, because missions do not arrive in batches. The mechanism for this rule is another rule's mechanism, and that is worth saying plainly rather than claiming an enforcement that does not exist.

Arm the loop first and the first thing it does at 3am is satisfy itself. The second-order reason is about evidence rather than cost — a self-certifying loop produces a RECORD of successes that becomes the input to every downstream mechanism, and bad outcome data is worse than none because it is actionable. Applied to Decision 7's synthetic landing page: that mission spans three of the four pack families and only one has a resolver today that is not the producing model, so if the acceptance test of the whole system carries a quality gate then the acceptance test is unresolvable — which is how a machine passes itself. This is a consequence of A3 and the 0.543 measurement, not a preference, and it respects Decision 6 rather than reopening it: all four families exist, they simply do not all have a resolvable exit on day one.

what_must_be_true: The founder accepts that year one produces a deliberately narrow machine: one mission at a time, one resolvable pack family dispatched unattended, and a balcony with one surface.

A worker reliably AUTHORS a `blocked` row with `clearable_by:` when it cannot reach a capability, instead of improvising around the gap and failing quietly. Nothing in this repo has ever tested whether it does, and the demand trigger depends on it.
`budget-guard.js` can actually be registered — it edits .claude/settings.json, which is irreversible tier and denied to the write tools, so it needs a founder action that is not yet authorised.

A definition exists for 'a mission that is not about the system', or the demand trigger is gameable by naming the harness a venture. Proposed: the mission's done-test must resolve against something outside this repository.
The task id lands on the first row of the event log and not the hundredth. CAST proved it cannot be retrofitted.
The founder is willing to see `unresolved` far more often than `pass` from the world verifier, and to read that as honesty rather than failure.
Refusals recorded in `.out-of-scope/` are honoured by future sessions, which requires the CI check — a refusal held only by this document decays silently within weeks.

refuse.why: design.js today sums four 0-10 axes into a `total` and sorts — the exact selector STARTUP-OS §7 forbids and the repo's own 0.543 measurement discredits. Weak judges are excellent finders and useless scorers. Mechanism: schema-lint refuses a numeric aggregation field in a judge output, the same shape as its existing refusal of `steps:` in a playbook stage. Smallest diff in this document, largest correction.

refuse.what: A done-test whose resolver is the producing model.
refuse.why: Protects every exit condition in the system. Mechanism: dispatch refuses a move whose goal names the producer as resolver.

An average wearing a costume, and it requires a trust model for opinions that cannot be validated at this volume. Auto-Co's Munger veto is the cautionary instance: prose in CLAUDE.md, all 14 personas at model: inherit, nothing checking disagreement occurred.

refuse.why: It has already happened here: qa-lead-pass.yml computed a stricter second answer than the classifier. Extend scripts/lib/classifier.js, never parallel it.
This is the wall that stops the org chart returning. Enforced by the persona holding no producing tools.

refuse.why: Transcripts are full of confidently-stated superseded beliefs and retrieval cannot distinguish a corrected belief from a current one, so this resurrects exactly what the supersession discipline exists to bury. Take as instrumentation, and only as a report a human reads — never as a context injection. Mechanism: a structural rule that no pack or agent references a transcript path, the PS-WORKFLOW-CONTAINMENT shape.

refuse.why: This is what makes 24/7 safe by type rather than by policy. Enforced by .claude/gates.yml: a `human` gate has no `run:` and writing one is refused.

refuse.why: Memory is where unwired code accumulates fastest, because nothing fails when memory is not read — proven here by 2,936 transcripts and no red test.

refuse.what: Disabling the sandbox globally to reach the second model family.
refuse.why: The sandbox is a guardrail against accident, and a 24/7 unattended loop is the accident case. Narrow per-command exemptions instead. Already enforced by npm run test:sandbox, which fails if `enabled` is flipped.

refuse.what: Template extraction, fleet rollout and multi-project operation.
refuse.why: Decision 4 already scopes this to one Mac and one founder; the extension is that a template of a system that has never run once is a template of nothing. Reopens when a second project exists AND the first has shipped an artifact that survived a world verdict.

A phase number makes its last item hostage to its first and makes abandonment expensive, because abandoning it means admitting the number was wrong. Nine phases, one venture task. Mechanism: WISH on its own; real only via the demand trigger, since missions do not arrive in batches.

build_order: 1. Register budget-guard.js. FORCED FIRST because it is simultaneously the rope (Decision 8), the stall ceiling, and the field's only working anti-circling detector — and arming a 24/7 loop without it is the most expensive mistake available. It is already built and verified by execution and registered nowhere. It needs a founder permission; registering it edits .claude/settings.json, which is irreversible tier.

2. A real task id on every event row. FORCED SECOND because it cannot be retrofitted — CAST proved it, and its cost figures now need a heuristic 60-second time-window join for want of a foreign key. Cost per surviving artifact, the retirement queue, founder-interventions-per-artifact and replay-based explanation all read this one field.

3. The non-producer done-test resolver. FORCED BEFORE THE LOOP, because a loop that self-certifies produces a record of successes that poisons every downstream mechanism, and bad outcome data is worse than none because it is actionable.

4. The loop, minimal. Ralph's shape: fenced by 1, recorded by 2, exited by 3. Plus a steer file polled at loop boundaries and a kill-switch file checked at every dispatch — two files, and the only answer to 'you cannot steer something already running'.

5. The `world` verifier, fail-closed. FORCED BEFORE A SECOND MISSION, because without it nothing distinguishes a mission that worked from a mission that finished. Expect `unresolved` far more often than `pass`, and say so in advance so it does not read as failure.
ALONGSIDE 1: `.out-of-scope/` with dates. Costs an hour, and everything after it depends on refusals being durable.
EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE CATALOGUE IS DEMAND-TRIGGERED — queued behind a mission blocked on its absence, not rejected.
open_questions: Is the demand trigger's bootstrap exemption one window with an expiry, or a standing allowance for 'harness work'? A standing allowance reproduces the last nine months exactly.
What counts as a mission that is not about the system? Without a definition the trigger is gameable by naming the harness a venture.

Does the founder accept a deliberately mediocre year one on design, video and content? The four pack families are decided; whether all four get resolvable exits before any is dispatched unattended is not.
What is N for P9 — how many balcony actions before a second surface is earned? It must be declared before the balcony is built or it will be set retroactively.

Which currently-granted hands should be REVOKED rather than merely not extended? Publish-to-TikTok, send-as-founder and remote code execution are live now; P10 governs only the next grant, and nothing in this document governs the existing ones.

Does refusing the evolutionary-search family contradict the founder's central complaint that the system loses creativity to playbooks? I argue no, because the creativity fix is killing the score (C1/C17), which is in scope and small. It is the closest call here.

Who resolves a rung-1 done-test ('a stranger understands it in five seconds') when there is no stranger? If the answer is the founder, the first mission is not unattended and Decision 7's acceptance test is weaker than it looks.
strongest_counter: The founder's diagnosis is that almost everything built is a stopping mechanism rather than a producing one, and this document is fourteen stopping mechanisms — the disease performed with more rigour than the disease usually manages. The sharper, structural form: a demand trigger can only fire for capabilities the system already has enough of to notice missing. A mission blocked on a hand that does not exist does not generate a `blocked` row; it generates a worker that tries something else, fails quietly, and gets abandoned. So the trigger risks running as a ratchet in the wrong direction, freezing the capability set at whatever it was the day the rule landed — which is exactly how organisations stop being able to do new things. My defence is partial: the trigger keys on `blocked`, which is AUTHORED with a `clearable_by:` naming what would clear it, not on `failed`, which is observed after the fact — and `clearable_by: <a capability that does not exist>` is a legitimate block. But that depends on workers reliably authoring blocks rather than improvising around gaps, and nothing here has ever tested whether they do. The second objection is the one I find harder: STARTUP-OS §1b already concluded the rebuild is small — six unwired, three absent, one working — so if most of the remaining work is WIRING, a refusal-heavy posture is fighting a war that was already won, and the moment needs execution rather than another filter. My answer is that ~420 options is precisely the condition under which a settled small plan becomes large again, and the filtering conversation is where that happens. But that answer is an assertion about this board's discipline and I cannot mechanise it.
